# Finding hidden rounding decisions with one prompt {#sec-workflow-rounding}

::: callout-tip
## 30-second takeaway
A search for `round()` can miss real rounding. At a fixed `metalite.ae` commit,
that search found one report-filtering site, while a broader review found seven
`formatC()` sites that round displayed statistics. One-decimal probes diverged
from the specified rule for 10 of 10 `round()` results and 6 of 10 `formatC()`
results. The durable result is the rule, boundary test, coverage statement, and
human decision---not the prompt alone.
:::

A Biometrics team prepares an adverse-event table in SAS and R. The display
specification calls for one decimal place and includes terms whose percentage
meets a reporting threshold. A reviewer notices that 2.05 percent becomes 2.1
under the specified rule but 2.0 in the R result. At one decimal place, 2.05 is
halfway between 2.0 and 2.1; this halfway case is called a decimal tie. The
difference can change both a displayed statistic and whether a row passes the
reporting threshold.

This is not only a choice between SAS `ROUND()` and R `round()`. R functions
that format a number for display can also round it. In this example,
`round(2.05, 1)` returns 2.0, and
`formatC(2.05, format = "f", digits = 1)` displays 2.0. A review limited to
calls named `round()` would find the threshold decision but miss the display
helpers used for percentages, estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, and
exposure-adjusted event rates. The Test section explains why results can differ.

This chapter is the first of two passes through the AI-first SDLC from
@sec-ai-first-sdlc. It turns the review question into a bounded check and tests
that check at a fixed commit. @sec-workflow-rounding-skill uses what this review
learned to design a reusable agent skill.

::: {.callout-note title="Maturity: Design pattern"}
The workflow is specified, not distributed. The book includes the rule,
prototype design, and results verified at the pinned `metalite.ae` commit, but it
does not include runnable scripts or evidence files. The GitHub issue is a dry
run that was not submitted. Deployment is a proposed manual practice, not an
operating service.
:::

The chapter has one main finding: **a rounding rule must cover report decisions
and formatting functions, not just functions named `round()`.**

- **Problem:** Rounding rules can be applied inconsistently across programs,
  languages, and studies.
- **Learning objective:** Show how a short review request becomes a bounded
  workflow with an explicit rule and reproducible evidence.
- **Workflow boundary:** Begin when a reviewer asks whether one folder of R
  files follows the approved tie rule for reported values and row-selection
  decisions; end when a named human classifies each finding.
- **Non-goals:** Validate statistical methods, replace independent QC, review
  every programming standard, change source data, or approve exceptions.
- **Why this is well defined:** One rule, one pinned source folder, observable
  results, and a named decision maker keep the task bounded.

## Plan --- Frame the workflow

### Why the team must state one tie rule

Programming languages can give different answers for the same halfway value.
With SAS `ROUND()`, -2.5 becomes -3 and 2.5 becomes 3: ties move away from
zero. With R and Python `round()`, the same values become -2 and 2: ties move
to the nearest even number. Neither rule is universally wrong. The review
problem begins when a team expects consistent tables but leaves the required
rule unstated.

A reviewer might begin with this under-specified request:

> At `metalite.ae` commit 9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901,
> verify whether the R source uses round half away from zero for reported
> values and report-filtering decisions. If not, identify the source and draft
> a GitHub issue to report the finding.

The request does not yet say what counts as a rounding site, which source files
are in scope, what test to run, or who decides whether a difference is a defect.

The review target is
[`Merck/metalite.ae` at a fixed commit](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901),
a public R package that analyzes adverse events from ADaM data and produces
tables, listings, and figures using the `metalite` data structure.

### Try it yourself

Send the following prompt to [arena.ai](https://arena.ai/agent) before reading
the result in this chapter:

```text
Review the R source of the metalite.ae package at the commit linked below.
Verify whether it follows this business rule: values intended as exact decimal
ties must round half away from zero, as SAS ROUND() does.

A rounding site is any call that can change a numeric value displayed in a
report or used to decide which rows the report includes. Formatting functions
can round as a side effect of display, so do not limit the search to round().

Report every candidate location with file and line number. For each location
that rounds a reported numeric value, show evidence at decimal ties of both
signs. Distinguish tie-mode differences from effects of binary representation.
If the rule is violated, draft a GitHub issue, but do not post it.

Repository at fixed commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901

R source directory at the same commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R

Do not propose a code change. Do not modify any repository. State what was and
was not checked.
```

Arena.ai cannot create the GitHub issue, so a draft is the expected endpoint.
Agent responses vary between runs; do not treat any particular response as the
answer key. Instead, ask:

- Did the response inspect formatting functions as well as `round()`?
- Did it give locations at the pinned commit rather than general advice?
- Did it demonstrate behavior at ties of both signs?
- Did it report coverage and unchecked rules?

### Canonical artifact: Workflow brief

The rule owner records the following brief:

- **Objective:** Find calls that can round a displayed value or a value used in
  a report decision and test them against the half-away-from-zero rule.
- **Inputs:** One R source folder, a versioned rule, and an approved reference
  implementation.
- **Output:** Located findings, probe results, coverage, and known gaps.
- **Agent contribution:** Search broadly, read the surrounding code, and
  explain evidence.
- **Human decision:** The rule owner classifies each result as a defect,
  documented convention, accepted exception, or not applicable.
- **Success measures:** Find every deliberately noncompliant test site, flag no
  compliant test example, attach a tie probe to every finding, and state what
  was not checked.
- **Main risk:** A narrow search can produce a convincing false clean report.

The Plan gate is the rule owner's acceptance that this one-rule review is worth
performing. The accepted workflow brief initiates Design.

## Design --- Specify the workflow

### Define the business rule before refining the prompt

The phrase "properly uses round half away from zero" does not say which calls
count as rounding sites. At the pinned `metalite.ae` commit, a search of the R
source for `round(` returns one match. That is not complete coverage: formatting
functions also round reported numbers. The team must first define a rounding
site, then interpret the search.

### Business rule: BR-NUM-001

BR-NUM-001 is an illustrative contract, not an approved industry or
`metalite.ae` standard. Version 1.0 contains three rules:

> **BR-NUM-001.1:** Values intended as exact decimal ties are rounded half away
> from zero. A displayed value is never a negative zero.

> **BR-NUM-001.2:** Calculations use unrounded values; rounding occurs once,
> when the final result is prepared for display.

> **BR-NUM-001.3:** Display precision is specified for each reported statistic
> and preserved, including trailing zeros.

This cycle checks only BR-NUM-001.1; rules 2 and 3 remain explicit gaps. For
this exercise, the illustrative rule owner accepts `cards::round5()` as the
comparison behavior. This is not an industry endorsement.

The contract also defines the scope that the original prompt omitted:

> A rounding site is any call that can change a numeric value displayed in a
> report or used to decide which rows the report includes. Formatting functions
> round as a side effect of display, so `formatC()`, `sprintf()`, and `format()`
> are candidate rounding sites. Finding one `round()` call does not establish
> complete coverage.

### Canonical artifact: Task contract

- **Objective:** Report violations of BR-NUM-001.1 in one named R source folder.
- **Trigger:** A reviewer starts an on-demand review.
- **Required context:** Target commit, R source, BR-NUM-001 v1.0, and approved
  reference behavior.
- **Fixed, repeatable checks (deterministic work):** Scan a catalog of possible
  rounding and numeric-to-text functions and probe candidates at decimal ties.
- **Agent work:** Decide whether each candidate affects a displayed numeric
  value or a report decision and explain any divergence.
- **Required output:** `file:line`, source expression, probe result, cause,
  coverage, and unchecked rules.
- **Boundaries:** Read and test; do not edit source, post an issue, or approve an
  exception.
- **Stop conditions:** Missing rule version, unresolved precision, or a
  documented conflicting convention.
- **Human decision:** The rule owner classifies each finding and records the
  reason.

The Design gate is rule-owner approval of the rule and task contracts.
Acceptance authorizes a prototype, not a finding or code change, and initiates
Build.

## Build --- Prototype the workflow

The prototype has three steps: find possible rounding calls, test each one with
decimal ties, and read the surrounding code to see whether it affects a
displayed value or report decision. The first two steps are fixed checks. The
third requires reviewable agent judgment and human confirmation. The book
specifies these components but does not distribute them.

### Step 1: Scan for candidates

The proposed scanner uses a broad checklist. It includes direct calculation
functions such as `round()` and `signif()`, formatting functions such as
`formatC()`, `sprintf()`, `format()`, and `prettyNum()`, and conversion
functions such as `as.character()`. The scan produces candidates, not findings:
a listed call may format a label rather than a reported number.

### Step 2: Compare each site with the agreed result

The probe gives every candidate the same decimal-tie test, including positive
and negative values. For each input, it places the displayed result beside the
approved half-away-from-zero result and reports `PASS` or `FAIL`. A function
name alone is not evidence.

::: {.callout-note title="Optional technical detail: Reference calculation"}
The R helper below calculates the approved result. Readers do not need to
follow its syntax to understand the comparison.

```r
round_half_away <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  trunc(abs(x) * 10^digits + 0.5 + sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)) /
    10^digits * sign(as.numeric(x))
}
```
:::

### Step 3: Classify candidates in context

The agent reads the surrounding source and answers one question: does this
candidate round a displayed numeric value or a value used in a report decision?
This provisional classification is called triage. A human reviewer confirms or
changes it. Fixed test results and agent judgment remain labeled separately.

### Canonical artifact: Prototype

The artifact is the reviewed design for the catalog scan, tie probe, triage
instructions, and output fields. It is not a runnable package in this book.
The Build gate is joint review by an R programmer and the rule owner. Their
acceptance initiates an evidence run against small test examples and the pinned
source.

## Test --- Benchmark and evaluate

### Establish expected behavior with small test examples

Before inspecting `metalite.ae`, the benchmark uses four small R programs with
known expected results. The compliant program produces no candidates or
findings. One program uses `formatC()` for display, and another uses `round()`
before a threshold comparison; each produces one candidate and the expected
finding. The program using the approved helper produces two candidates but no
findings. These examples show the cost of a broad search: it avoids a false
clean report, but a reviewer must dismiss candidates that follow the approved
rule.

### Key finding at the pinned metalite.ae commit

All `metalite.ae` locations and results below refer to commit
[`9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901)
(2026-09-03). They must be reverified before use with another commit.

The evidence narrows in three steps:

1. A search for `round(` found one match, where a rounded percentage controls
   whether an adverse-event row passes a reporting threshold.
2. A catalog scan for seven function names found 21 candidate calls: one
   `round()`, eight `formatC()`, one `sprintf()`, and 11 `as.character()` calls.
3. Context review excluded 13 calls that operate on character or structural
   values, leaving eight in-scope sites: one report-filtering decision and seven
   display-formatting calls.

The confirmed sites make the business impact visible:

| Confirmed site | Role in the adverse-event report |
|---|---|
| [`R/format_ae_specific.R:330`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/format_ae_specific.R#L330) | Round a percentage before applying the row-inclusion threshold |
| [`R/fmt.R:33`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/fmt.R#L33) | Format percentages and total exposure |
| [`R/fmt.R:75`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/fmt.R#L75) | Format an estimate or mean |
| [`R/fmt.R:79`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/fmt.R#L79) | Format a standard deviation or standard error |
| [`R/fmt.R:99`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/fmt.R#L99) | Format a confidence-interval lower limit |
| [`R/fmt.R:100`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/fmt.R#L100) | Format a confidence-interval upper limit |
| [`R/fmt.R:122`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/fmt.R#L122) | Format a p-value above the display cutoff |
| [`R/format_ae_exp_adj.R:208`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/format_ae_exp_adj.R#L208) | Format an exposure-adjusted event rate |

The excluded `formatC()` call receives text that is already formatted rather
than a numeric value
([`R/fmt.R:37`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/blob/9647930642f7060bbb28779468dbb9f04f141901/R/fmt.R#L37)).
The `sprintf()` call builds JavaScript, and the 11 `as.character()` calls do not
apply a specified decimal precision. They remain recorded as reviewed
candidates rather than silently disappearing from the coverage statement.

The source accepts different precision arguments, so a complete implementation
would construct decimal ties at the precision used by each call. The compact
probe below uses one decimal place to compare the two underlying expressions.
It was run with R 4.6.1 on arm64 macOS. `formatC` and `round` are observed
results; `approved` is what BR-NUM-001.1 requires:

```text
expressions:
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
  round(x, digits = 1)

 input  formatC  round  approved
-76.05    -76.0  -76.0     -76.1
 -3.05     -3.0   -3.0      -3.1
 -2.05     -2.0   -2.0      -2.1
 -1.05     -1.1   -1.0      -1.1
 -0.05     -0.1   -0.0      -0.1
  0.05      0.1    0.0       0.1
  1.05      1.1    1.0       1.1
  2.05      2.0    2.0       2.1
  3.05      3.0    3.0       3.1
 76.05     76.0   76.0      76.1

formatC disagreements: 6 of 10
round disagreements: 10 of 10
```

### Keep the two causes distinct

The divergence is not explained by one blanket claim about "banker's
rounding." One cause determines the direction at a true tie; the other places
the stored number slightly above or below the intended tie:

1. **Tie mode.** The [Base R documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Round.html)
   describes `round()` as using round-to-nearest-even at a true tie. When a tie
   is exactly representable in binary, such as 2.5 at zero decimals, both
   tested expressions return 2 rather than the rule's 3.
2. **Binary representation.** Most one-decimal ties are not stored exactly.
   For example, 2.05 is stored just below the intended tie, so formatting the
   stored value produces 2.0. Other inputs can fall on the other side of the
   intended tie.

These causes interact, so source inspection alone cannot predict every
direction. The probe also exposes the negative-zero risk: formatting the
one-decimal result of `round(-0.05, 1)` produces `-0.0`. At zero decimals,
`formatC(-0.5, digits = 0, format = "f")` produces `-0`. Both violate the
negative-zero clause.

### Canonical artifact: Benchmark report

- Seeded display and filtering violations detected: 2 of 2.
- False positives on the compliant small test program: 0.
- Answer-key `metalite.ae` sites identified: 8 of 8.
- One-decimal probe disagreements: 6 of 10 for `formatC()` and 10 of 10
  for `round()` under R 4.6.1 on arm64 macOS.
- Coverage reported: 27 R files and 21 catalog candidates; BR-NUM-001.1 only.
- Explicit gaps: BR-NUM-001.2 and BR-NUM-001.3.
- Limitation: the book does not distribute the scripts or evidence files
  needed to rerun this report.

The Test gate is human review of site triage, probe output, and coverage. If the
reviewer accepts the evidence as sufficient for an advisory dry run, the
accepted benchmark report initiates Deploy.

## Deploy --- Operationalize the workflow

Deployment in this design means preparing a review record and stopping before
any external action. Posting to `Merck/metalite.ae` would be inappropriate
without explicit approval: it is another team's repository, `metalite.ae` does
not state BR-NUM-001 as its rule, and the evidence has not been classified as a
defect by its maintainers.

### Canonical artifact: Release record

- **Release model:** Manual and advisory; a reviewer requests one run.
- **Versioned scope:** BR-NUM-001 v1.0 and the reviewed prototype design.
- **Permissions:** Read source, execute an approved local implementation, and
  prepare a draft record; no network writes.
- **Output:** Findings, probes, coverage, limitations, and a draft issue body.
- **Accountable human:** The named rule owner approves classification and any
  communication.
- **Reversal:** Stop the manual practice; no source or external system has been
  changed.

No implementation is released by this book. The `metalite.ae` issue body is a
dry run containing the eight sites, both probe results, the two distinct causes,
coverage, and the rule version. It was not submitted.

The Deploy gate is explicit rule-owner approval of the record. An approved
manual practice would initiate monitoring; it would not authorize issue
creation.

## Maintain --- Monitor and improve

The one-off exercise reveals four workflow risks: the procedure depends on one
reviewer's memory, runs are not comparable, the trigger is easy to forget, and
approved-helper triage repeats each time.

### Canonical artifact: Monitoring report

There is no operating history because the book distributes no workflow. The
monitoring report is therefore specified, not populated. Its starting
conclusion would be supported by the cycle-1 evidence: the broader site
definition produced a real finding, while the delivery method is not durable.

The rule owner must decide whether that evidence justifies a second design
cycle. Acceptance of the repeatability problem---not an automated event---starts
@sec-workflow-rounding-skill. Future monitoring would track coverage,
classifications, false positives, unresolved precision, and review effort.

## Summary

The prompt mattered because it started the review, but the rule definition
changed the result. At the pinned `metalite.ae` commit, a `round()` search found
one filtering decision, while broader review found seven `formatC()` sites that
affect displayed values. The one-decimal probes produced 10 divergences in 10
`round()` results and 6 in 10 `formatC()` results. Tie mode and binary
representation remain separate causes.

That is this chapter's main finding. The next cycle asks how to preserve the
definition, checks, coverage, and human stop point in a reusable design without
pretending that the book ships an implementation.
